newsitem.title: USA: Rockwell's profit up as it completes transition.
newsitem.headline: Rockwell's profit up as it completes transition.

text.p: Rockwell International Corp. said Tuesday that operating earnings for its second quarter rose 28 percent as it completed its transformation from an aerospace and defense company into an electronics manufacturer.

Rockwell, which makes industrial automation systems, semiconductors and avionics and communications equipment, said net income from continuing operations climbed to $155 million, or 72 cents a share, from $121 million, or 55 cents a share, in the year-ago period.
Overall net income, including discontinued businesses, dropped by 12 percent to $189 million, or 87 cents a share, from $214 million, or 98 cents a share, a year earlier.
Sales rose by 6 percent to $1.9 billion from $1.8 billion, led by double-digit growth in its automation and avionics and communications businesses.

"We were very very pleased to have the first quarter of the new electronics-focussd Rockwell come out of the chute with the good results that we had," Chairman Don Beall said in an interview. "I think you can say Rockwell has been transformed."

Rockwell's latest quarterly earnings excluded the automotive components business which saw quarterly earnings drop to $34 million from $39 million a year ago. Rockwell said in March it would spin off the unit to shareholders in a move seen by analysts as an attempt to boost earnings.
The prior year's quarter also included earnings of the aerospace and defense business which was sold to Boeing Co.
Rockwell, which is based in Seal Beach, Calif., said revenue growth was spurred by its industrial automation unit, where sales rose 10 percent to $1.1 billion from $1.0 billion.

"What is clearly driving our performance is the strong market conditions worldwide for automation and our strong results in avionics, and we expect both of those to continue and they are more than covering the flattish period for our semiconductor business," Beall said.
Semiconductor sales for the quarter fell by 15 percent -- from a record quarter last year -- as it switched over to producing new, higher-speed modem chip sets.

Beall said the semiconductor business will be flat this year, adding that while the long-term prospects for the business were rosy he declined to speculate when the unit would return to strong growth.
Despite the transition in the semiconductor business, Beall said he is maintaining his previously stated goal of 15 percent earnings growth annually.
Beall, just returned from a nine-day business trip to China, said that region will fuel much of Rockwell's growth.
"Asia-Pacific is clearly our fastest growing region, and we see lots of opportunities for growth in Asia-Pacific, particularly in China," he said.
While Rockwell is unlikely to divest any of its remaining businesses, it will remain active in acquisitions, Beall said.
"We continually make small and moderate-sized acquisitions ... and you can expect more," Beall said. "I'm not predicting any blockbusters."
Rockwell's stock closed at $65.625 a share, up $3.25, on the New York Stock Exchange.
